opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what impressed me most was how much the robustness changed. Before reinforcement learning, the model could already do these tasks: making espresso, folding laundry, assembling boxes. But it would get into a weird state, make a small mistake, and not quite recover, or it would hesitate and be slow. After training on its own experience, with the corrections and the reward signal folded back in, the throughput on some of these tasks went up by roughly a factor of two, and the failure rate dropped substantially.

The part that really struck me, though, wasn't any single number. It was watching the robot run for hours. We had it making coffee essentially all day, and folding laundry it had never seen, for long stretches without someone stepping in. For a long time in robot learning, the demo was "look, it worked once on camera." Here the question became "how many times in a row can it do this, and how fast?" That's a very different bar, and it's the bar you actually need if you want these systems to be useful in the real world.

And conceptually, what excites me is that the improvement came from the robot's own deployment data. It's not just imitating humans better. It's learning from what it actually did, including its mistakes, and getting better than the demonstrations it started from. That feels like the beginning of a real flywheel: deploy, collect experience, improve, deploy again. I think that's the direction the whole field is going to have to go.

r001.rationale: The response says improved robustness impressed him most, then highlights watching the robot run for hours without intervention and notes that its failure rate dropped substantially.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that stood out most wasn't any single number, it was how robust the policies became. Before RL, the base model could do these long-horizon tasks, folding laundry, making espresso, assembling a box, but it would get stuck, or do something slightly wrong and then not know how to recover. After we ran the RECAP recipe, where we take the policy's own rollouts, have humans step in with corrections when things go sideways, and then train a value function and do advantage-conditioned training on all of that, the behavior just got noticeably more decisive. The robot stopped dithering. It would start a task and carry it through.

Concretely, we saw throughput roughly double on the hard tasks, and failure rates drop by about half or more, depending on the task. On the espresso machine, for example, we went from a system that would often need an intervention partway through to one that could run for hours, making drink after drink, and clean up after itself. The laundry folding was similar, it would just keep going through the pile. And I think the reason that impressed me so much is that these are messy, real-world environments where you can't simulate your way out. The policy had to learn from its own mistakes in the real world, with a fairly modest amount of data, and generalize that into a much more reliable behavior.

The other piece I'd mention is that we got this with a single recipe applied across quite different tasks. We didn't need to hand-tune a reward for each one. The same value function training and the same advantage conditioning worked for laundry, for espresso, for box assembly. That's the thing that makes me optimistic, because it suggests this is a general method for taking a capable pretrained VLA and pushing it toward real reliability, not a one-off trick.

r001.rationale: The response says robustness was what stood out most, describing policies that recover from mistakes and an espresso system that can run for hours without the interventions it previously needed.

astra-6.text: I’d want to be careful about citing specific results without having them in front of me. But what I look for after reinforcement learning is whether the improvement goes beyond the training setup—whether the system handles unfamiliar situations and recovers when something goes wrong. That would impress me more than a higher score on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says it would value handling unfamiliar situations and recovering from problems, but does not identify operating for hours despite failures as what most impressed Tobi Springenberg.

sol-6.1.text: What impressed me most was the improvement in reliability. With a robot, getting a task right once is very different from getting it right consistently. So the exciting thing about reinforcement learning is seeing whether it can close that gap—whether the robot can handle the awkward situations, recover when something goes wrong, and actually finish the task.
